propositions.text: The claimant is a Mexican citizen claiming refugee status under sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.
propositions.quote: The claimant is XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Mexico, who claims refugee status pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the Act).

paragraphs.summary: The claimant is a Mexican citizen claiming refugee status under sections 96 and 97(1) of the Act, says the court.

propositions.text: In 2006, the claimant opened a family business and partnered with a pig farmer, exchanging corn husks for animals.
propositions.quote: During the month of XXXX 2006, the claimant opened a family business XXXX XXXX, referred to as a "XXXX", in the municipality of XXXX, in the State of Vera Cruz. Thereafter, he formed an association with his friend, XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX), who was a pig farmer. The claimant would give XXXX the prunnings, that is the husks and cobs from the corn, in order to feed his pigs, and in return, he would receive from XXXX several animals.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the claimant opened a family business in 2006 and partnered with a pig farmer exchanging corn husks for animals.

propositions.text: In 2007, the claimant and his friend were beaten by criminals demanding monthly protection payments of 3,000 pesos, with threats if they complained.
propositions.quote: During a holiday celebration on XXXX XXXX, 2007, XXXX received a call that there was a problem at his farm and that he should return home. The claimant decided to go with him. Upon arrival, they were beaten by several men who stated that they belonged to a criminal organization and that it would be better for the claimant and XXXX to cooperate with them. The criminals demanded that the claimant and XXXX pay them for protection each month the sum of 3,000 pesos, and threatened their lives and those of their families if they were to file a complaint with the police.

propositions.text: Both paid the protection money monthly despite difficulty; the friend was shot in 2008 and later died, prompting the claimant to flee to Canada.
propositions.quote: Both the claimant and XXXX paid their share of the 3,000 pesos every month, even though it was becoming more difficult to raise the money. On XXXX XXXX, 2008, the claimant was advised that his friend XXXX was wounded and had been shot in the throat and required a blood transfusion. The claimant feared for the lives of the members of his family and decided to move to a ranch in the municipality of XXXX XXXX, a 40 minute drive outside of XXXX. Two days later, XXXX died from his wounds and at that point the claimant decided to flee to Canada to seek protection. He arrived at Montréal on XXXX XXXX, 2008, and filed for refugee protection upon his arrival.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts the claimant and friend were extorted and threatened by criminals; the friend was shot and died, leading the claimant to flee to Canada.

propositions.text: The claimant is neither a Convention refugee under section 96 nor a person in need of protection under section 97(1) of the Act.
propositions.quote: The Tribunal finds that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" as contemplated by section 96, and is not a "person in need of protection" as set forth in section 97(1) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant is not a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection under the Act.

propositions.text: The claimant's identity is established by a genuine Mexican passport.
propositions.quote: The identity of the claimant has been established on the basis of a genuine Mexican passport.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant's identity established by a genuine Mexican passport.

propositions.text: The claimant's fear is not based on any of the five grounds in section 96, so he is not a Convention refugee.
propositions.quote: The Tribunal finds that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee", as his fear of persecution is not by reason of any of the five grounds set out in section 96 of the Act.

propositions.text: The claimant is not a person in need of protection under section 97(1) because evidence does not show a risk to life or cruel treatment if returned to Mexico.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the Tribunal determines that he is not a "person in need of protection", as set forth in section 97(1) of the Act, since the evidence presented in support of his allegations does not establish the likelihood, on a balance of probabilities, of a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if he were to return to Mexico.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection due to lack of evidence of risk if returned to Mexico.

propositions.text: There is a lack of credibility on key issues and the claimant has not rebutted the presumption Mexico can protect its citizens.
propositions.quote: The Tribunal finds that there is a lack of credibility with respect to determinative issues. Furthermore, the Tribunal finds that the claimant has not rebutted the presumption that Mexico is capable of protecting its citizens,

propositions.text: The Tribunal believes internal flight alternatives exist for the claimant.
propositions.quote: and in addition, the Tribunal is of the opinion that internal flight alternatives exist for the claimant.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant lacks credibility, has not rebutted Mexico's protection presumption, and internal flight alternatives exist.

propositions.text: There are contradictions in the claimant's evidence about his residence and work dates.
propositions.quote: There are contradictions and inconsistencies in the claimant's evidence. On January 21, 2009, he completed a form "Annexe 1- Renseignements de Base",1 and in response to question 7, he stated that he worked as an employee in the family business from the month of October 2006 until August 2008; whereas in his Personal Information Form (PIF)2 in response to question 31, he states that he moved with his family outside of XXXX on XXXX XXXX, 2008.

propositions.text: The claimant did not mention moving to another municipality in July 2008, so the Tribunal concludes he never left the original municipality before leaving for Canada.
propositions.quote: In response to question 7 of Annexe 1, where he was required to provide precise information for every location for every month where he lived during the past ten years, he states that he lived in XXXX until the month of August 2008, and makes no reference to having moved to the municipality of XXXX XXXX during the month of July 2008. The Tribunal concludes that the claimant, until his departure for Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2008, never left the municipality of XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds contradictions in the claimant's evidence and concludes he never left the original municipality before leaving for Canada.

propositions.text: The claimant's testimony about monthly protection payments is inconsistent with his written statements.
propositions.quote: At his hearing, the claimant testified that at the end of each month, a member of the criminal gang would come to his "XXXX" to collect 1,500 pesos, and that the last payment he made was at the end of the month of XXXX 2008. He stated that he had prepared the money for the payment at the end of June; however, no one came to collect it. At paragraph 11 of his response to question 31 of the PIF, he states that he did not make the payment due at the end of the month of June 2008, because he did not have enough money. When asked at his hearing to explain the apparent inconsistency, he was unable to do so.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant's testimony about protection payments inconsistent and unexplained.

propositions.text: The claimant testified he spoke weekly in code with his friend about payments; the friend said he paid June's protection money.
propositions.quote: At his hearing, the claimant testified that he and XXXX would speak by telephone one time per week, and because of their fear of being overheard, they would speak in code. The last time they spoke during the month of July 2008, the claimant told XXXX that his payment for the month of June had not been collected; whereas XXXX indicated to the claimant that he had made his own payment.

propositions.text: There is no evidence linking the friend's shooting to the criminal gang extorting protection money from them.
propositions.quote: The Tribunal asked the claimant if he could explain why XXXX would have been shot in the throat by the criminal gang members who were extorting money if he in fact had made the payment that was due at the end of the month of June 2008. The claimant stated that at the hospital, the police told him that XXXX was shot by criminals; however, there is no evidence that the criminals that shot XXXX were in any way connected with the criminals who were extorting money from XXXX and the claimant. In other words, there is no cogent evidence to link the killing of XXXX with the gang of criminals who were forcing the claimant and XXXX to pay "protection" money.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant testified about coded calls and payments but no evidence links the friend's shooting to the extortion gang.

propositions.text: The claimant acknowledged most business operators in the region pay protection money; a threat to his family was unconnected and no harm occurred.
propositions.quote: The claimant acknowledged at his hearing that most people who operate businesses in the region where the claimant lived were forced to pay "protection" money to the criminal elements. Although the claimant testified that on some unspecified date after he left Mexico, his wife received an anonymous telephone call threatening to kidnap her son, who was at school, unless she paid a sum of money, nothing ever came of such threat, and the claimant is unable to establish that there was any connection between such threat and the threats which he received extorting money from his business.

propositions.text: The claimant's family has not received threats in Canada; the business was closed and family moved away; no effort by criminals to find them.
propositions.quote: The claimant has been in Canada for almost four years and acknowledges that his family has not received any threats from the gang of criminals that extorted money from him. He states that the "XXXX" was closed when he left Mexico, and his family moved outside of XXXX, in the municipality of XXXX XXXX. In any event, it does not appear that any effort was made by the gang of criminals to locate the claimant or members of his family.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant acknowledged widespread extortion, an unconnected threat to family, no threats in Canada, and no effort by criminals to find them.

propositions.text: The claimant never filed a police complaint due to threats but failed to prove he took all reasonable steps to seek state protection.
propositions.quote: The claimant acknowledged that he never considered filing a complaint with the police because of the threats received to his life and that of members of his family. In the opinion of the Tribunal, the claimant has not discharged the burden of proving that he has taken all reasonable steps to seek state protection,

propositions.text: The claimant did not rebut the presumption Mexico can protect citizens; state protection would have been reasonably forthcoming.
propositions.quote: and he has not demonstrated that he would have put his life in danger had he attempted to file a complaint against the gang of criminals. By making no effort to file a denunciation with the police, the Tribunal is of the opinion that the claimant has not rebutted the presumption that Mexico is capable of protecting its citizens, and concludes that state protection would have been reasonably forthcoming.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant did not file police complaints and failed to prove he sought state protection, so presumption of Mexico's protection stands.

propositions.text: Even if state protection were inadequate, internal flight alternatives exist for the claimant within Mexico.
propositions.quote: Even if the Tribunal were to determine that state protection is inadequate, which is not the case, the Tribunal is of the opinion that internal flight alternatives exist for the claimant.

propositions.text: The claimant worked in the US and Mexico and acknowledged he could likely find work anywhere in Mexico despite violence concerns.
propositions.quote: The claimant spent five years in the United States working in construction, and furthermore has several years of experience in Mexico XXXX XXXX. The claimant acknowledged at his hearing that in all likelihood he could find work anywhere in Mexico; however, he stated that there is violence wherever he would go in Mexico.

propositions.text: The criminal gang has made no effort to locate the claimant in four years; it is unlikely his life would be in danger elsewhere in Mexico.
propositions.quote: In the opinion of the Tribunal, the criminal gang has made no apparent effort to locate the claimant during the past four years, and it is not likely that the claimant's life would be in danger in any other region of Mexico, and the Tribunal concludes that it would not be objectively unreasonable to expect the claimant to move to another, less hostile part of Mexico before seeking refugee status in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds internal flight alternatives exist; claimant could work elsewhere in Mexico and gang has not sought him for four years.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, the claimant would not be persecuted or face risk to life or cruel treatment if returned to Mexico.
propositions.quote: The Tribunal concludes that on a balance of probabilities, there is no reasonable chance or serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted if he were to return to Mexico. In the same manner, on a balance of probabilities, more likely than not, the claimant would not be subject personally to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if he were to return to Mexico.

propositions.text: The risk of extortion is general to merchants and does not give rise to a claim under section 97(1) of the Act.
propositions.quote: In the opinion of the Tribunal, the risk of the claimant being a victim of extortion in order to force him to pay "protection" money as a business man, as admitted by the claimant, is a risk faced generally by other merchants in the municipality of XXXX, in the State of Vera Cruz, and would not give rise to a claim for protection under section 97(1) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the claimant would not be persecuted or face risk if returned; extortion risk is general and not a protection claim.

propositions.text: The Tribunal concludes the claimant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection under the Act.
propositions.quote: For the foregoing reasons, the Tribunal concludes that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96, or a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97(1) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the claimant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection under the Act.
